# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review of "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

**Overall:** This is a valuable follow-up. It answers the persistence question that every earlier document left open. It also lands two well-founded corrections:
- **To the meta-analysis:** all four of its long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours.
- **To the re-analysis:** a gain does survive record-based output, randomisation, stricter hours measurement and two years of follow-up.

The body of the report is careful. The problems are mostly in how results are summarised and interpreted:
- The Summary overstates the decline in the gain.
- The decline may partly reflect control offices improving, not treated offices fading.
- The mediation result is less independent and less "confirmed" than claimed.
- What the system logs actually measure needs specifying.

## Arithmetic checks (pass)

- **Output per hour.** Output per hour = (1 + change in output per FTE) ÷ (1 + change in hours).
  - Timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so **+9.8%** ✓
  - System logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so **+8.5%** ✓
- **Halden continuers.** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a fall of 13.4% ✓. Then 96.8 / 86.6 gives **+11.8%** ✓.
- **Meetings.** The difference-in-differences is (3.9 − 7.4) − (7.0 − 7.2) = −3.3 hours. This matches the 9-month exploratory gap ✓.
- **Mediation shares.** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓.
- **Counter-arm costing.** Restoring throughput after an 11.4% fall needs about 1/0.886 ≈ 13% more staff, so "12%" is close. A 9% rise in cost per contact implies labour is about three-quarters of total cost. That assumption should be stated.

## Main issues

### 1. The Summary mixes hours measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a log figure.
- **Like-for-like (timesheets):** 12.5% → 9.8%, a relative decline of about 22%.
- **As the Summary phrases it:** about 32%.

Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" falls between the two. The headline should use the timesheet comparison and report the log figure separately.

The change itself also has no confidence interval. The 9-month interval (6.9 to 18.4) and the 24-month interval (4.6 to 15.2) overlap almost entirely. So the data fit "some fading" but cannot distinguish it from no change. The report should give the CI for the difference.

### 2. Part of the "decline" may come from control offices improving

From month 15, two of the seven control offices ran a meeting audit and gained 4.1% in output per hour. That raises the control average by roughly 4.1 × 2/7 ≈ 1.2 points. On its own, that could account for about 40% of the 2.7-point fall in the treated-versus-control gap.

The report presents the meeting audit as a hint that gains could be had without cutting hours. It does not consider the audit as **contamination of the control group**, which biases the 24-month estimate downward and makes fading look larger than it is. Two further analyses would help:
- Re-estimate excluding the two audit offices, or with an indicator for them.
- Report whether the idea spread from treated offices, since cluster randomisation was meant to prevent exactly that.

A related oddity: the control mean for meeting time is 7.0 hours at month 24. If the two audit offices stayed at 5.0, the other five must average about 7.8, which is *above* the control baseline of 7.2. Either meeting time drifted up in the other control offices, or the audit offices drifted back toward their old levels. The authors should say which.

### 3. The mediation test is registered but not independent

**Same units, overlapping data.** The meetings hypothesis came from 7 treated offices. The "confirmatory" test uses the same 7 offices (plus controls) and overlapping months. Registering at month 11 guards against choosing the analysis after seeing the results. But the test is not an out-of-sample replication. "Survives a registered test" is accurate. "Confirms" in the Summary is not.

**Mediator confounding.** Meeting reduction was not randomised. Managers who cut meetings may also have improved other things. The limitations section acknowledges this, which sits uneasily with "confirms."

**Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the information available. Office-months are clustered, and there are 14 offices. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for that design. The authors should report the method used, and with so few clusters, a wild-cluster bootstrap or permutation interval.

**Precision of the fatigue pathway.** Its interval (2 to 34%) only just excludes zero.

### 4. What do the system logs measure?

The logs record "active log-in time on the case-management system." That raises three questions.

**Are meetings in the logs?** If log time covers case-work only, it excludes meetings by construction. Then:
- Output per log-hour is not simply a stricter version of output per timesheet-hour. It measures a different denominator.
- The meetings mediation changes meaning. Cutting meetings cannot raise output per *case-work* hour by freeing time. It could only do so through fewer interruptions or better focus. That is a different mechanism from "removing low-value time," the interpretation offered at nine months.

**Can the figures be reconciled?** Timesheet hours fell about 4.5 hours a week (12% of 37.9), and meeting time fell 3.3 hours. If logs excluded meetings, an 11% fall in log hours (roughly 3.3 hours on a base of about 30) would not fit inside the timesheet total.

**Is the log measure really "stricter"?** Log-in time can overcount, for example when staff are logged in but idle. It can also undercount phone calls, paper work and meetings.

The authors should report log-hour levels, not just percentage changes, and state exactly what activity the logs capture.

### 5. Costs are still not addressed

Cost per case closed has not been reported in either the 9-month or the 24-month report. At full pay, output per FTE is −3.4% (CI down to −8.0%). Timesheets show hours falling 12% against a scheduled 20%, which implies continued overtime of roughly 3 hours a week.

The county costed the counter arm, but not case-processing. For an employer deciding whether to extend the scheme, this is the missing number.

### 6. The Halden follow-up

- **Response selection.** Only 14 of the 23 record-holding organisations responded. Non-response may be concentrated among organisations that reverted or did poorly. The authors' "upper bound" framing is appropriate, and "survivors twice over" is well put.
- **Who reverted.** One of the three reverting organisations is a **marketing agency citing client deadlines**. Marketing would normally be coded as discretionary. The Summary's "client-facing or coverage obligations" blurs this. It suggests that deadline-bound client work can behave like coverage-bound work, which complicates the meta-analysis's two-category scheme.
- **Correcting the record.** A Halden author co-signs this report. Given that, it is a natural place to address the re-analysis's finding that 7 of the 9 withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, contrary to the original working paper. The report is silent on this.

## Minor points

- **Timing of the estimates.** Say whether the 24-month figures are month-24 values or averages over a window, and whether the 9-month and 24-month estimates use the same window length.
- **Resignations.** These were not a registered outcome at nine months. Say whether they were added to the follow-up protocol.
- **Baseline meeting data.** The 9-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. Explain where the baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2) come from, presumably retrospective extraction from calendars, and how complete they are.
- **The audit offices' gain.** The +4.1% in the two audit offices is an uncontrolled before-and-after comparison. Seasonality is one alternative explanation; the authors already flag that the comparison is uncontrolled.

## Where the five documents now stand

| Question | Current best answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8–10% on actual hours, persisting to 24 months in one randomised trial. The measured fading may be partly artifact (control contamination). |
| Output per employee, discretionary | Slightly below control (about −2% to −3%). The hours cut is mostly but not fully offset. |
| Coverage-bound work | Output and service fall. The randomised arm was terminated, and restoring service costs about 9% more per contact. |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported. |
| "Sector-general" | Not supported. |
| "No decay" | Not supported. The long-run evidence in the meta-analysis came entirely from uncontrolled, scheduled-hours studies. |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction is the largest measured pathway. Evidence is from one trial, the same units that generated the hypothesis, and is sensitive to what logs measure. Fatigue is a smaller contributor. |
| Gain without cutting hours? | Unknown. No trial arm reorganised without cutting hours. |
| Cost per unit of output | Unreported for discretionary work. |

The obvious next study would add a third arm that reorganises work, by auditing meetings and cutting low-value reporting, without reducing hours. That design is the only way to separate the hours effect from the reorganisation it prompts. I can sketch its design and power requirements if useful.
